questions.question: After a car accident a 32-year-old female passenger is brought to the accident and emergency department with a severe head injury. No other injuries have been reported from the ambulance crew at the scene. On admission her GCS is 7, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, the patient is spontaneously breathing room air with O2 saturation 98%; the arterial blood gas analysis reveals pO2 10.7 kPa, PCO2 4.9 kPa, pH 7.46 and HCO3- 26 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step while still in the Emergency Department?
options: Give pre-emptive mannitol for cerebral protection prior to transport to the ICU
Nothing, but leave for immediate brain CT scan
Lie the patient head-down to place a central venous line through the internal jugular vein
questions.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less normally warrants tracheal intubation but, even when coma is less severe, a deteriorating state of consciousness provides additional evidence for critical care admission.
questions.topic: GCS 7 head injury - indication for rapid sequence intubation

questions.question: Characteristics of the vegetative state (VS) or Unresponsive Wakefulness State include:

statements.label: B
statements.text: Being defined as persistent if present over one month after initial brain injury

questions.explanation: Vegetative state (VS) / Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS) describe those patients who 'awaken' from their coma - meaning they recover the ability to open their eyes, spontaneously or on stimulation - but remain unaware of self or environment, showing only reflex motor responses. In short, VS = arousal without awareness.
questions.topic: vegetative state / unresponsive wakefulness syndrome characteristics

questions.question: Regarding the assessment of best motor responses by applying noxious stimuli, which of the following statements are true?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pressure to the eye-bulb is preferred above pressure to the supraorbital notch

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deep pinprick in the abdominal area can be used to assess abnormal flexion responses

statements.label: C
statements.text: Forced pinching in the upper arm can be used to assess abnormal flexion responses

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pressure to the nail-bed of the finger can elicit spinal reflexes

questions.explanation: Recommended noxious stimuli (in order of least harmful, especially if repeated assessment is required) are squeezing the trapezius muscle, pressure to the supraorbital notch, and the temporomandibular joints (performing a jaw thrust). Pinching the nipple or rubbing the sternum should preferably not be used as noxious stimuli, and pressure to the nail beds is not recommended, as this can elicit spinal reflexes which may confuse the assessment. Neurological responses must be carefully noted; these can be withdrawal or posturing reflexes, including any evidence of lateralisation of signs, as well as purposeful or non-purposeful spontaneous movements. Stereotyped extension of the upper limbs was formerly called decerebration, and abnormal flexion of the upper limbs was formerly called decortication; these should now simply be called extension or abnormal flexion responses.
questions.topic: noxious stimuli technique for motor response assessment

questions.question: The primary arousal structure in the brain (the ascending reticular activating system) is found in following anatomical region:
questions.explanation: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS), the primary arousal structure, is located in the upper pons and in the lower midbrain, in the posterior part of the upper two-thirds of the brainstem. A ventral pathway projects ARAS to the hypothalamus and to the basal forebrain; a dorsal pathway projects to the reticular nuclei of the thalamus; and a third pathway projects directly into the cortical regions.
questions.topic: anatomical location of the ascending reticular activating system

questions.question: A 21-year-old male is brought to the accident and emergency department after driving off the road. He is spontaneously breathing with 10 L/min of oxygen on a facemask. At admission his blood pressure is 95/45mmHg, heart rate 115/min, SpO2 92%, with a deep and regular respiratory rate of 35/min and GCS is 7. What type of cause of coma is most likely?
options: An immune-mediated cause such as an acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis
questions.explanation: The evaluation of the respiratory pattern may provide clues to the cause of the coma and to the localisation of the brain pathology (Validation of a new coma scale: the FOUR score, Wijdicks et al, Ann Neurol 2015). This deep, regular (Kussmaul-type) breathing pattern suggests a metabolic origin of coma, such as diabetic ketoacidosis or other severe causes of metabolic acidosis.
questions.topic: respiratory pattern as clue to cause of coma

questions.question: Wernicke's encephalopathy is an uncommon form of coma. It's characteristics include:
questions.explanation: An important cause of acute or subacute delirium, Wernicke encephalopathy is a neurological disorder induced by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. It is the most important encephalopathy due to a single vitamin deficiency, and presents with the classic triad of ocular findings, cerebellar dysfunction, and confusion.

questions.question: Important primary laboratory tests in patients with unexplained comatose state include:
questions.explanation: Besides standard laboratory tests (electrolytes, glucose, leukocyte count, liver enzymes, coagulation studies, renal function, arterial blood gas analysis, toxicological screening and serum osmolality), it is common to assess serum ammonium level in every unexplained comatose state because of its therapeutic implication - control of increased intracranial pressure and the need for specific treatments.
questions.topic: primary laboratory tests in unexplained coma

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the investigation of brainstem reflexes are correct?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Disconjugate eye positions may suggest the presence of a brainstem lesion

statements.label: B
statements.text: Disconjugate eye positions may result from partial anaesthesia from sedative medications

statements.label: C
statements.text: Corneal reflex testing is made by using saline drops to prevent corneal lesions

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tracheal suctioning in mechanically ventilated patients allows testing of the cough reflex

questions.explanation: Disconjugate eye positions may suggest the presence of a brainstem lesion, though partial anaesthesia from sedative medications can also produce disconjugate gaze. Corneal reflex testing is performed using saline drops to avoid corneal lesions; it is quick to test, and its absence suggests a pontine lesion and may carry major prognostic value. Tracheal suctioning in mechanically ventilated patients also allows testing of the cough reflex.

questions.question: Which of the following clinical signs would lead you to suspect cocaine overdose as the cause of coma?
questions.explanation: Seizures, strokes, and coma can accompany cocaine overdose. According to a study by Treadwell and Robinson, cocaine can lead to strokes and coma, or even sudden death, in persons with no cardiovascular risk factors; cocaine may lead to the formation of life-threatening clots by constricting the cerebral vasculature. Reference: Treadwell SD, Robinson TG. Cocaine use and stroke. Postgraduate Medical Journal. 2007;83(980):389-394.
questions.topic: clinical signs of cocaine overdose causing coma

questions.question: Regarding the Glasgow Coma Score, which of the following are true?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Involves testing the pupillary response to light

statements.label: B
statements.text: Involves testing the best verbal response

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assesses all important components of coma assessment

questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) remains the most widely used coma assessment scale. However, it suffers from some limitations. First, GCS may not always be reliable in mechanically ventilated patients, particularly with regard to the verbal component. Second, GCS lacks assessment of an important component of coma assessment in ICU patients, i.e. testing of brainstem reflexes.
questions.topic: limitations of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.question: Consciousness is a state characterised by self-awareness and by the ability to respond to external factors. It can be sub-divided into:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Arousal (Wakefulness): clinically defined as the ability to open eyes

statements.label: B
statements.text: Awareness: the patient is able to 'voluntary' interact with the examiner or the environment

statements.label: D
statements.text: Minimally conscious state: awareness but no arousal

questions.explanation: Consciousness is defined as a state of awareness of self and environment and the ability to respond to environmental factors. It can be divided into arousal (wakefulness) and awareness. Arousal (wakefulness, alertness, or vigilance) is clinically defined as the ability to open the eyes, spontaneously or on stimulation; it is regulated by the intact function of the Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS), a large sub-cortical area located in the brainstem, the diencephalon (hypothalamus and thalami), the basal forebrain, and their projections to the cerebral cortex. Awareness (awareness of self and environment, i.e. the content of consciousness) is clinically defined as the observation of the patient's 'voluntary' interaction with the examiner or the environment; it is regulated by the intact, interrelated functions of the cerebral cortex and its subcortical, mainly thalamic, connections, and self-awareness can only be approached through complementary explorations. Brain death corresponds to an irreversible cessation of all brain functions, including brainstem functions; once assessed clinically, complementary work-up is frequently mandatory depending on jurisdiction. Coma is clinically defined as a state of unresponsiveness in which the patient does not open the eyes and shows no signs of awareness of self or environment - i.e. coma is neither arousal nor awareness. Minimally conscious state (MCS) is characterised by the presence of arousal with inconsistent but reproducible goal-directed behaviours, e.g. response to command, verbalisation, or visual pursuit, with communication largely impaired; patients emerge from MCS once they are able to functionally use objects and/or communicate on two consecutive clinical assessments - i.e. MCS is arousal with minimal and partial or fluctuating signs of awareness.
questions.topic: definitions of arousal, awareness, coma and minimally conscious state

questions.question: The FOUR score for testing of altered consciousness (Full Outline of UnResponsiveness score) of ICU patients includes:
questions.explanation: The Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) score is a coma assessment scale that includes brainstem reflexes. It tests four components of brain function - eye response, motor response, brainstem reflexes, and respiration pattern - and has been validated extensively in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It has been translated into several languages and can be used by nurses. The FOUR score is able to detect clues to brain death, herniation, locked-in syndrome and minimally conscious state.
